title: Deterministic Almost-Linear-Time Gomory-Hu Trees
authors: Amir Abboud (Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel), Rasmus Kyng (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Jason Li (Carnegie Mellon University, USA), Debmalya Panigrahi (Duke University, USA), Maximilian Probst Gutenberg (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Thatchaphol Saranurak (University of Michigan, USA), Weixuan Yuan (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Wuwei Yuan (ETH Zurich, Switzerland)
abstract: Given an undirected, weighted graph $G=(V%, E,w)$, a Gomory-Hu tree or cut tree (Gomory and Hu, 1961) is a tree $T$ over the vertex set $V$ such that for every pair of vertices $s, t\in V$, the $(s, t)$ min-cut in $T$ is also an $(s, t)$ min-cut in $G$ and has the same value. In this article, we give the first deterministic almost-linear-time algorithm for constructing a Gomory-Hu tree. Our algorithm runs in $m^{1+o(1)}$-time, where $m$ denotes the number of edges in the input graph $G$; this is clearly optimal up to the $m^{o(1)}$ term in the running time. Prior to our work, the best deterministic algorithm for this problem dated back to the original algorithm of Gomory and Hu that runs in $nm^{1+o(1)}$ time using current max-flow algorithms. In fact, our algorithm is also the first almost-linear-time deterministic algorithm for even simpler problems, such as finding the k-edge-connected components of a graph. Our new result hinges on two separate and novel components that each introduce a distinct set of de-randomization tools of independent interest:Our new result hinges on two separate and novel components that each introduce a distinct set of de-randomization tools of independent interest: a deterministic reduction from the all-pairs min-cuts problem to the single-source min-cuts problem incurring only sub-polynomial overhead, and a deterministic almost-linear time algorithm for the single-source min-cuts problem.

The classic algorithm by Gomory and Hu from the 1960s
is a deterministic reduction to n − 1 invocations of (s, t)min-cut and (using current max-flow algorithms) achieves a
runtime bound of nm1+o(1) . The reduction can be viewed as
a divide-and-conquer strategy that has recursion depth up to
n − 1, where each level comprises (s, t)-min-cut subproblems
on graphs containing O(m) edges in total. Over the last
few years, a long line of work [16]–[22] has developed a
powerful framework that follows this reduction but enforces
Õ(1) recursion depth,1 thereby resulting in an m1+o(1) -time
algorithm.
These recent results rely on identifying a pivot vertex r ∈ V
and a corresponding set of vertex-disjoint (v, r)-min-cuts Sv
for some vertices v ∈ V , such that each set Sv as well as
the vertices not in any Sv are only a constant fraction of |V |.
This translates to subproblems in the next recursive level that
are a constant fraction smaller, and eventually, to a recursion
depth of Õ(1). But, how do we identify a pivot vertex? These
results show that, in fact, a constant fraction of the vertices
are valid pivots by the above definition. This then allows
an algorithm to sample such a vertex uniformly at random.
Once a pivot r is sampled, the algorithms use a variety of
advanced techniques to compute disjoint sets of (v, r)-mincuts Sv with the properties described above, again heavily
relying on randomization. These cuts are then used to define
the subproblems at the next layer of recursion and yield the
overall recursive algorithm.

extension of Karger’s duality-based technique of obtaining a

Abstract—Given an undirected, weighted graph G = (V, E, w),
a Gomory-Hu tree or cut tree (Gomory and Hu, 1961) is a tree T
over the vertex set V such that for every pair of vertices s, t ∈ V ,
the (s, t) min-cut in T is also an (s, t) min-cut in G and has the
same value.
In this article, we give the first deterministic almost-linear-time
algorithm for constructing a Gomory-Hu tree. Our algorithm
runs in m1+o(1) -time, where m denotes the number of edges in
the input graph G; this is clearly optimal up to the mo(1) term
in the running time. Prior to our work, the best deterministic
algorithm for this problem dated back to the original algorithm of
Gomory and Hu that runs in nm1+o(1) time using current maxflow algorithms. In fact, our algorithm is also the first almostlinear-time deterministic algorithm for even simpler problems,
such as finding the k-edge-connected components of a graph.
Our new result hinges on two separate and novel components
that each introduce a distinct set of de-randomization tools of
independent interest:
• a deterministic reduction from the all-pairs min-cuts problem to the single-source min-cuts problem incurring only
sub-polynomial overhead, and
• a deterministic almost-linear time algorithm for the singlesource min-cuts problem.
Index Terms—Gomory-Hu trees, graph algorithms, deterministic algorithms.

I. I NTRODUCTION
For a pair of vertices s, t in a graph G, the (s, t) edge
connectivity λG (s, t) is the value of a minimum (s, t)-cut,
or equivalently, that of a maximum (s, t)-flow. Finding the
(s, t) edge connectivity for all pairs of vertices in a graph is
a fundamental problem. In a seminal result in 1961, Gomory
and Hu solved this problem on undirected (weighted) graphs
by proposing a tree data structure defined on the vertices of the
graph that encodes an (s, t)-min-cut for each vertex pair s, t
in the graph [2]. This is called a Gomory-Hu tree (GHT REE)
or cut tree of the graph. Since their introduction, GHT REEs
have been widely studied in combinatorial optimization [3]–
[12] and have found applications in diverse domains such

We replace this randomized framework with a deterministic
algorithm based on a recent data structure from [27]. By augmenting dynamic trees [28] in a non-trivial way, our algorithm
deterministically maintains an implicit representation of the
Steiner tree packing. We then construct a vertex sparsifier
using the cut information of the packing, and subsequently
compute a small collection of guide trees from this vertex
sparsifier that deterministically satisfy the same guarantees as
the previous randomized construction (in the randomized case,
the guarantees hold with high probability). In addition to being
a key component of our GHT REE algorithm, we hope that
the vertex sparsifier that we construct will be of independent
interest.
As an aside, we note that substituting our new algorithm
for computing guide trees into the (randomized) algorithm
of [22] gives an almost-linear-time algorithm for GHT REE
that is arguably more modular and simpler that the original
construction. This makes progress on the final open question
in [22] that asks for a “simple” reduction from Gomory-Hu
trees to max-flow calls.

A. Our Results
In this article, we close the gap between the randomized
and the deterministic complexity of the GHT REE problem.
Our algorithm runs in m1+o(1) time, which is optimal up to
the mo(1) term. We show:
Theorem I.1. Given an undirected, weighted graph G =
(V, E, w) with polynomially-bounded, non-negative edge
weights, there is a deterministic algorithm that computes a
Gomory-Hu tree T of G in m1+o(1) time, where m is the
number of edges in G.
This theorem positively answers the first open question in
[22]. As a corollary, it also yields the first deterministic almostlinear-time algorithm to compute k-edge-connected components of an undirected graph.

Roadmap. After describing related work in the next section,
we give an overview of the main techniques in the subsequent
sections of the paper. We start by giving a reduction from
Gomory-Hu trees to solving the problem of single-source mincuts (SSMC) in Section III. We then give a reduction that
reduces the SSMC problem to the problem of finding guide
trees in Section IV. Finally, we show how to construct guide
trees efficiently in Section V. The full technical details of the
results presented in this extended abstract appear in [1].

Theorem I.2. Given an undirected graph G = (V, E) and a
positive integer k ≥ 0, there is a deterministic algorithm that
computes the k-edge-connected components of G in m1+o(1)
time.
B. Our Techniques
There are two key technical contributions that help realize
Theorem I.1 and might be of independent interest.

II. R ELATED W ORK
Global min-cut. The global min-cut of a graph is also
an (s, t)-min-cut of minimum value across all vertex pairs
s, t ∈ V . Thus, a global min-cut of an undirected graph can
be obtained from a GHT REE in O(n) time.
For more than a decade, the global min-cut problem served
as a prominent example for showing the power of randomness
in graph algorithms. It was a basic problem where the fastest
randomized algorithms—the Karger-Stein algorithm via edge
contractions [29] and Karger’s tree packing algorithm [23]—
were faster than the best-known deterministic algorithms by
a factor of n. A celebrated 2015 paper by Kawarabayashi
and Thorup [24] gave an Õ(m) deterministic algorithm to
the problem for unweighted, simple graphs, while introducing
novel expander-based arguments for analyzing min-cuts. Later,
almost-linear and near-linear time algorithms were obtained
for weighted graphs [25], [30], [31] via powerful new techniques such as the isolating cuts framework [16], [25]. Notably, both the expander-based arguments and the isolating cuts
framework were key ingredients in the recent (randomized)
results on GHT REE.

Deterministic Pivot Selection. First, we consider the aforementioned challenge of deterministically finding one of the
Ω(n) pivots in the input graph. Our main structural insight
in resolving this problem is the following: we show that for
the largest integer k with the property that there exists a kconnected component C of size at least 34 |V |, every vertex
in C is a suitable pivot. We run a binary search to compute
k, and give a new deterministic algorithm for computing C
that is inspired by the expander-based de-randomizations for
global min-cut from [24], [25].
Deterministic Construction of Guide Trees. The second
major challenge is that of sampling a guide tree from a Steiner
tree packing, which, in turn, is computed by a Multiplicative
Weights Update (MWU) algorithm. A key difficulty is that
the size of the support of this packing can be much larger
than m. Because of this reason, the m1+o(1) -time randomized
algorithm of [22] had to operate on an implicit packing,
e.g., obtained via the Randomized MWU framework [26].

to obtain an (s, t)-min-cut for a given pair of vertices s, t ∈ V .
It is well-known that this problem is the dual of the (s, t)max-flow problem, and an (s, t)-min-cut can be obtained in
linear time from an (s, t)-max-flow. The (s, t)-max-flow/mincut problem is one of the most well-studied problems in graph
optimization, and a long history of research spanning decades.
Nevertheless, an almost-linear-time algorithm for this problem
was obtained only recently [32] via a suitable interior point
method (IPM) that reduces the problem to solving the socalled min-ratio cycle problem on a dynamic graph. They
then present an efficient data structure that solves the minratio cycle problem on dynamic graphs generated by the
IPM. Further research has simplified, de-randomized, and
generalized these results in [33]–[35].
We note that all algorithms for GHT REE reduce the problem
to solving max-flow instances. Indeed, the current record of
nm1+o(1) for deterministic GHT REE algorithms is also a
corollary of applying the almost-linear time deterministic maxflow algorithm in [33] to the reduction of Gomory and Hu [2].

In this work, we introduce a deterministic version of this
pivot selection framework. To our knowledge, the only previous result along these lines was by Abboud, Krauthgamer,
and Trabelsi [17], who put forth the dynamic pivot technique
and used it to de-randomize their quadratic-time algorithm for
simple graphs. Unlike us, they do not use structural insights
to deterministically find a good pivot; instead, their method
is based on an efficient algorithm for switching from one
candidate pivot to another, when the former is revealed as
being inadequate. Unfortunately, their technique does not seem
general enough to be usable for weighted graphs. Moreover,
it seems to inherently incur a quadratic factor in the running
time, and is therefore insufficient for getting almost-linear time
bounds. Finally, we would like to remark that the randomized
pivot idea is also used in a recent paper of Kolmogorov
that aims to simplify the recent algorithmic developments
for GHT REE, and make them more amenable to practical
applications [55].

k-edge-connected components. In the k-connected component problem, the objective is to find the coarsest possible
partition of the vertex set V such that each vertex subset in
the partition is k-edge-connected. (Recall that a set of vertices
is k-edge-connected if at least k edges have to removed to
disconnect any pair of vertices in this set.) This problem can be
solved by constructing a Gomory-Hu tree and identifying the
k-edge-connected components in the tree by removing edges
of weight less than k.
For k = 1, the problem is trivial: simply use BFS or
DFS to report the connected components of the graph in
O(m + n) time. But, somewhat surprisingly, the problem
already becomes non-trivial when k = 2. Starting with the
seminal work of Tarjan [36] in 1972, there has been a large
body of literature obtaining fast algorithms for k ≥ 2 [37]–
[42].2 In fact, the first linear-time algorithm for k = 4 was
obtained as recently as 2021 [44], [45] and that for k = 5
in 2024 [46]. Finally, the case of arbitrary k was addressed
a few months back in the work of Korhonen [47], who gave
2
an O(m) + k O(k ) n-time algorithm for the problem. Clearly,
this algorithm is inefficient when k is super-constant, even
for k = O(log n). In parallel to this line of work, Bhalgat et
al. [48] (see also [49]) gave an Õ(mk)-time algorithm for
this problem, based on what they called a partial Gomory-Hu
tree. Their result has the advantage that it can be applied for
super-constant values of k, but the algorithm is randomized.
In summary, we note that in spite of much research on the
problem over many decades, there is no known deterministic
algorithm for finding the k-edge-connected components of a
graph that runs in (almost) linear time, for general k.

III. C OMPUTING G OMORY-H U T REES VIA SSMC
As in all previous algorithms for Gomory-Hu trees, we work
with a terminal version where we compute the Gomory-Hu
tree of G only over a set of terminal U ⊆ V . This is convenient
for computing a Gomory-Hu tree recursively (where artificial
vertices are added).
Definition III.1 (Gomory-Hu U -Steiner Tree). Given an undirected, weighted graph G = (V, E, w) and a set of terminals
U ⊆ V , the Gomory-Hu U -Steiner tree is a weighted tree T
on the vertices U , together with a function f : V 7→ U such
that the following holds:
• For any s, t ∈ U , consider any minimum-weight edge
(u, v) on the unique st-path in T . Let U ′ be the vertices
of the connected component of T \ (u, v) containing s.
Then, f −1 (U ′ ) ⊆ V is an (s, t)-min-cut in G, and its
value is wT (u, v), the weight of the edge (u, v) in T .

Informal Lemma III.1 (Decomposition Lemma). There is a
deterministic algorithm that runs in m1+o(1) time and returns
a pivot r ∈ U and a collection S = {(Sv , v)} of sets Sv ⊂ V
and vertices v ∈ U \ r such that the following hold:
1) for every (Sv , v) ∈ S, Sv is a (v, r)-min-cut,
2) the sets Sv are vertex-disjoint, and
3) there exists a constant C such that for every set Sv , we
haveS|Sv ∩ U | ≤ C·|U |, and the remaining vertices V ′ :=
V \ (Sv ,v)∈S Sv also satisfy |V ′ ∩ U | ≤ C · |U |.

Recall that our goal is to compute a U -Steiner GHT REE
in deterministic almost-linear time. At a high level, we follow
the basic divide-and-conquer approach introduced by Gomory
and Hu [2], which we describe first.

The original Gomory-Hu algorithm [2]. For any two vertices
s, t ∈ U , we find an (s, t)-min-cut S ⊆ V (we use one side
of the cut to identify it). Let GS be the graph obtained from
G by contracting V \ S into an artificial vertex. Then, find
the Gomory-Hu (U ∩ S)-Steiner tree TS on GS . Similarly, for
T = V \S, find a Gomory-Hu (U ∩T )-Steiner tree TT on GT .
The U -Steiner Gomory-Hu tree is then obtained by “joining”
TS and TT by an (s, t) edge with value equal to the (s, t)min-cut value δG (S) = λG (s, t). Correctness of this algorithm
follows from the observation that min-cuts are nesting, that is,
for any x, y ∈ U , we can find an (x, y)-min-cut X such that:
• if x, y ∈ S, then X ⊆ S, and
• if x, y ∈ T , then X ⊆ T , and
• if x ∈ S, y ∈ T (or vice versa), then either X ⊆ S or
X ⊆ T . In fact, either X = S or X is also an (s, x)min-cut or a (y, t)-min-cut.
In the above algorithm, it can be ensured that the graphs at
the same recursion level have a total of O(m) edges. Thus,
for recursion depth d, the algorithm runs in time d · m1+o(1)
time since an (s, t)-min-cut can be obtained deterministically
in m1+o(1) time on an m-edge graph. Unfortunately, the
recursion depth in this basic framework can only be bounded
as O(n), which yields an nm1+o(1) time algorithm.
A first guess toward improving the runtime in the above
framework is to search for an (s, t)-min-cut that is relatively
balanced, which will automatically improve the recursion
depth. But, unfortunately, there are graphs that do not have
any balanced (s, t)-min-cuts (e.g., a star graph).
However, in [48], [54] it was observed that for some
constant C > 1, one can find a pivot r ∈ U , together with a
set S consisting of disjoint (v, r)-min-cuts Sv such that each
Sv contains at most |U |/C terminals, and V \ ∪Sv ∈S Sv also
only contains at most |U |/C terminals. The disjointness of

Review of Randomized Techniques. The central contribution
of [21] was to define and show the existence of guide trees
and to construct them in randomized almost-linear time. They
showed that:
There is a fractional collection P of U -Steiner trees
T1 , T2 , . . . , Tk (these are trees that span the terminal set
but not necessarily the entire vertex set of G) such that
sampling O(log n) trees proportional to their fractional
values yields a collection of O(1)-respecting guide trees.
• An (approximate) packing P can be found by using the
multiplicative weights update (MWU) framework. This
reduces the problem to m1+o(1) calls to an algorithm that
finds the U -Steiner tree T in G of minimum length w.r.t. a
length function ℓ (given by MWU) that is monotonically
increasing in each coordinate, and undergoes m1+o(1)
updates.
• The minimum-length U -Steiner tree problem can be
solved via a decremental single-source shortest paths
(SSSP) data structure that can be thought of as a dynamic
version of Mehlhorn’s approximate Steiner tree algorithm
[58].

As mentioned earlier, we also give the first deterministic
almost-linear time algorithm for the SSMC problem.
Theorem IV.1 (Single Source min-cuts). Given an undirected
weighted graph G = (V, E, w) and a source terminal s, we
can compute the pairwise min-cut values λ(s, t) for all vertices
t ̸= s in deterministic time m1+o(1) .
To establish this theorem, we follow closely the randomized
algorithm by [19], which, in turn, is heavily inspired by [21].
The last algorithm can be thought of as a clever generalization
of Karger’s spanning tree packing algorithm for global min-cut
[23] to packing a collection of Steiner trees (called guide trees)
for finding Steiner min-cuts and further to SSMC. Effectively,
this algorithm reduces the SSMC problem to computing a set
of guide trees, which are defined as follows:

However, the above reduction glosses over many technical
complications that one has to overcome, especially for a
weighted graph: even an approximate fractional packing P
comprises at least Ω(m) trees, which implies that the trees
cannot be stored explicitly (for U = V , the support size would
be Ω(mn)).
They bypassed the barrier by using “randomized MWU”
[26], [59]: in each iteration, they still find a near-minimumlength U -Steiner tree Ti under the current lengths, but instead
of increasing the lengths on all edges of Ti as in standard
MWU, they increase lengths only on a carefully chosen
random subset of its edges. The resulting random length
trajectory — and thus the implicit fractional packing — stays
very close to what standard MWU would produce, while
ensuring that each edge is selected for update only Õ(1)
times in expectation. This avoids the Ω(mn) bottleneck from
explicitly listing all Ti in weighted graphs.
To make this work in almost-linear total time, the algorithm
must report the chosen random subset in time proportional to
its output size. They design an involved data structure that
supports exactly this output-sensitive reporting under length
increases and plugs into the rest of the MWU loop. This is
very complicated and spans more than fifty pages [22].

Definition IV.2 (Guide trees). For an undirected, weighted
graph G = (V, E, w), we say a cut A ⊆ V is k-respected by
a tree T (with V (T ) ⊆ V (G)) if there are at most k edges in
T with exactly one endpoint in A.
For terminals U ⊆ V with source s ∈ U , a collection of
trees T is called a k-respecting set of guide trees, if for every
t ∈ U \ {s} with λG (s, t) ≤ 1.1 λG (U )3 , some tree T ∈ T
k-respects some (s, t)-min-cut.
The main idea of the reduction is to recursively construct a
(k−1)-respecting set of guide trees T ′ from a k-respecting set
T (or extract the (s, t)-min-cut value via a direct computation).
While this reduction is randomized in [19], we show that it
can be de-randomized using standard techniques.
Since each step of this recursion incurs a constant blowup,
it is crucial that k is a constant. Showing that such a collection
of guide trees (with constant k) can be computed deterministically in almost-linear time poses a central challenge (especially
for weighted graphs) that is addressed in the next section.

Naturally, the algorithm above is not sufficient for our purpose
as it requires going over the supports of T1 , T2 , . . . , Tk , which
might result in a large runtime, and does not guarantee the

However, we maintain the forest R as in Informal
Lemma V.1 in a dynamic Euler tour data structure described in

Maintaining the U -Steiner Subtree in a forest via augmented dynamic trees. In general, we cannot hope to explicitly maintain the subtree M U in a separate data structure as
a single edge insertion/deletion in M may lead to Ω(n) edge
insertions/deletions in M U . Instead, in our implementation,
we follow the approach of [28] to decompose M . Following
their nomenclature, we refer to edges that are in R ⊆ M as
solid and edges in M \ R as dashed.
Now consider processing edge updates to M (from the
batch of updates, so U might be temporarily disconnected).
For deletion of an edge (u, v), it suffices to find the last edge
on the intersection of all paths from u (respectively v) to every
terminal u′ (v ′ ) in the subtree of u (v) (after removing the edge
(u, v) from M ) and to make it dashed. For insertion of an edge
(u, v), where (u, v) now appears on a u′ v ′ -path in M for u′
(v ′ ) being a terminal in the subtree of u (v), we need to convert
each edge on the u′ v ′ -path to a solid edge. Potentially, there
are many dashed edges on such a path. However, by using
arguments similar to the analysis in [28], we can show that
this operation turns at most O(log n) edges from dashed to
solid on average.

global edge connectivity λH . Applying Gabow’s algorithm
on H returns a feasible tree packing on H with size λH
and packing value λH /2 in deterministic time Õ(λH mH ).

packing algorithm to H yields no(1) guide trees as desired.

In this paper, we presented the first almost-linear-time
deterministic algorithm for the Gomory-Hu tree problem. This
bridges the gap between the deterministic and randomized
complexity of this problem, and is, in fact, the first improvement in deterministic algorithms for this problem since the
60-year old result of Gomory and Hu [2]. Along the way,
we provided several conceptual simplifications to the previous
randomized techniques that we hope will add to the existing
toolkit in graph algorithms. The natural next step is to obtain
a near-linear-time algorithm, i.e., that runs in Õ(m) time, but
such an algorithm (even a randomized one) is still unknown
even for a single pair (s, t)-min-cut, and would be a major
breakthrough.
